happened: Three Republican commissioners left the FEC: Sean Cooksey (January 2025), Allen Dickerson (April 2025) and Trey Trainor (October 2025). This left the commission without a quorum. On February 11, 2026, President Trump nominated two Republicans, Andrew Woodson and Ashley Stow, to replace Dickerson and Trainor. In late October 2026 the FEC's website still listed only two commissioners, so the nominees had not taken office.

key_dates.event: Dickerson leaves; the FEC loses its four-member quorum.
President Trump nominates Andrew Woodson and Ashley Stow.

closeness: Matches the step of naming Republican replacements. Whether the nominees share the departing commissioners' views on regulating political activity was not confirmed, and no nominee for Cooksey's former seat was found.
uncertain: No Senate hearing or vote was found; the newest detailed source is a March 2026 CRS report, and the FEC's commissioner page was checked in October 2026. Woodson works at the Wiley Rein law firm and Stow worked with Trainor, according to news reports.

In 2025 the department cut the staff of its Public Integrity Section, which handles election crimes, and said it was reviewing parts of the Justice Manual, but no new campaign finance charging policy was announced.

happened: No instruction telling the Justice Department to consult official FEC interpretations, such as advisory opinions and past enforcement actions, before prosecuting was found. The Justice Manual's campaign-finance section does not mention FEC rulings, and since June 2025 its separate requirement to consult the Public Integrity Section before such cases has been suspended "while revisions are ongoing."
closeness: No action matched. The June 2025 suspension concerns internal consultation, not consideration of FEC interpretations. See ch29-003 and ch29-004.
uncertain: The revised Justice Manual section had not been posted as of this check, so its final content is unknown. The suspension notice is dated June 2025.

FEC, filed in February 2026, the FEC told the court in April 2026 that it lacked a quorum to defend the case. The National Republican Senatorial Committee joined as a defendant and won dismissal in federal district court in Washington, D.C., on September 15, 2026.
closeness: No matching action found. In at least one case the FEC could not defend itself and a private party, not the Justice Department, took on the defense.

happened: No law removing the FEC's power to go to court on its own was found among laws enacted through October 2026. A February 18, 2025 executive order (EO 14215) said the President's and Attorney General's legal views bind independent agencies, including the FEC, but it did not take away the FEC's litigating authority. A Democratic Party lawsuit against the order's effect on the FEC was dismissed on June 3, 2025 for lack of standing.
closeness: No matching action found. The 2025 order increases presidential control over the FEC's legal positions, which is related but different.
uncertain: A web search found no 2025-2026 bill or presidential request to end the FEC's independent litigating authority.

happened: Congress has not raised contribution limits. On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in NRSC v. FEC that federal limits on political party spending coordinated with candidates violate the First Amendment, removing one type of limit on parties.

key_dates.event: Supreme Court decides NRSC v. FEC (No. 24-621).

legal: Supreme Court, NRSC v. FEC, No. 24-621 (June 30, 2026), 6-3. Justice Kavanaugh wrote for the Court, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett; Justice Kagan dissented, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Jackson. The Court held the party coordinated-expenditure limits in 52 U.S.C. 30116(d) violate the First Amendment and overruled its 2001 Colorado II decision.
closeness: Partial. The ruling removed limits on party spending coordinated with candidates, which the chapter also criticizes, but limits on contributions to candidates and parties remain in place. The change came from a court, not Congress or the administration.
uncertain: How the FEC has put the ruling into practice was not checked. The vote and holding were confirmed from the Court's preliminary print.
